COVENANT

Movement of Hope

Rome 1997

Movement of Hope, at the Institute of the Daughters of St Anne

PRESENTATION

This year’s journey of faith, illumined by the theme of “COVENANT” (a biblical category that comes before that of “HOPE”), will be carried out with the help of the Celebrations in this booklet.

The theme, which runs through the whole Bible, takes account of the great covenants of God with humanity:

with Noah

with Abraham

with Moses (the Sinai covenant) with David (the royal covenant)

in the Prophets (the covenant of love)

and with Jesus (the new and eternal covenant)

These units, made up of various closely connected parts, are set out in the sequence of the individual Celebrations. Each Celebration aims to help us grasp God’s “initiative” towards humanity and creation, at all the fundamental stages of the History of Salvation.

A privileged place is given, as a vantage point, to the spiritual group identified with the Remnant of Yahweh, to which St Anne belonged, Mother of Mary Immaculate, whose charismatic and spiritual continuator in the Church is Mother Rosa.

From the viewpoint of this group of men and women faithful to God, we contemplate the historical beginning of the Covenant up to the time of its definitive fulfilment in Christ.

By deepening the theme step by step through the series of Celebrations, we shall find it easier to see how each Covenant is not exhausted in a single person (for example, Abraham, Moses…), but is completed and interwoven with the other covenants and moves towards the end times.

The Celebrations, 63 in all (55 for the weekly meetings, 8 for the monthly retreats), are structured in such a way that, starting from listening to the Word of God, through the passage of Scripture chosen each time, we pass by means of a brief key to its interpretation to a comparison with the same experience of God in the life of Mother Rosa, and then to the response of personal adherence to the Lord through the questions for catechesis or reflection that follow.

As in the experience of the people of Israel, each Celebration should help us become aware of the Covenant that God wants to establish, and continues to establish, with us in Christ Jesus, and of the commitment that must spring from it in each one of us.

For the members of the Movement, to deepen this biblical category of the Covenant is a twofold gift: to rediscover it as a fundamental reality in their own lives as Christians, and to live it as spiritual heirs of the Little Remnant of Israel.

INTRODUCTION

“Many times you offered your covenant to men and women…” – so we pray in the Fourth Eucharistic Prayer.

It is true: many times God began, or took up again, his dialogue with man. And always in order to offer him a “path” of communion of life with himself.

“And when through disobedience he lost your friendship, you did not abandon him to the power of death, but in your mercy you came to the aid of all, so that those who seek you might find you.” So, in that same anaphora, we go on praying: “…and through the prophets you taught us to hope for salvation!”

This is what we should learn every day: “to hope for salvation”. To hope for that meeting with the Lord, to seek that divine heart which can give rest to our anxieties and our troubles. At Holy Mass we ask for it after the Our Father: “Deliver us, Lord, from every evil… grant us peace… and we shall live secure from all disturbance.”

For this reason it will be good to meditate on that “Covenant”, “offered to us many times” and so many times ignored or rejected or, worse, despised!

It will be good to contemplate the forbearance and patience of our God, so kind in stooping down to our whims and our ingratitude.

How truly we feel like groaning with the psalmist and, sighing, exclaiming: “What is man, O Lord, that you care for him?”

All the sons and daughters of Adam are a breath, it is true, and yet you, Lord, remember them and have made them little less than… a “god”!

This was precisely the beginning of the divine proposal: the creation of Adam, of man. Made of “clay”, yet lifted up to the face of God. Created to be “king” and to become the image and reflection of the invisible God, a sharer “in the divine nature”.

But after the rejection and… the divine bitterness, God looks upon Noah. In that “ark” was the seed of a new humanity and the trembling of God’s heart: “I swear by myself: humanity will never again be destroyed!”

But once more man would want to walk towards “heavens” other than the one offered by God.

Like that of Babel, how many “towers” have we tried to build throughout history? And how often have we met only with confusion, shame, loneliness? With his own “clay”, man learns to know violence, division and death.

But God’s wonder is the wonder of a child. He will take refuge in the lap of a lonely old man. With tenderness he will entrust that covenant to him: “Do not be afraid, Abraham, I am your shield, your path, your long life. I shall be your blessing, your fulfilment, your descendants… Do not be afraid, I shall make you peoples and nations!”

And that “pact” would truly reveal God’s faithfulness through the descendants of Abraham: Isaac, Jacob, those twelve sons, the fruit of the blessing, would form the seed of a numerous people, the people whom God would acquire for himself in order to become its bridegroom and father and shepherd and most tender ally.

“You shall be my people and I will be your God!”

But that generation winked at other… lovers!

They wanted other kinds of covenant: “A ‘king’ like the other nations, a ‘god’ to lead us like those of other peoples.”

Once again man returned to his “clay”, to his history without “heaven”. A scattered flock, a stubborn and still dispersed people.

“They have abandoned me to follow other ‘gods’; they have rejected me so that I should no longer reign over them”: this was God’s lament to Samuel.

A young shepherd took up that sigh of God: “Let no one lose heart. I used to look after my father’s flock, and the Lord who rescued me from the claws of the lion and the claws of the bear will rescue me also from the hands of this Philistine who has insulted the armies of the living God!”

Zeal for the armies of the living God would make David the “king” who would please God’s heart. With him, with his descendants, the covenant would be renewed and preserved.

But… the folly of the human heart, again obstinacy, again forgetfulness, unfaithfulness and desertions…

The anguished voices of the prophets will achieve nothing, or very little: “Return, come back to the Lord our God. He will heal us!”

The nation will be destroyed, and with it the Sanctuary, the delight of the holy city. Stripped of everything, Israel will no longer be a people. It will no longer have a land.

It will be led into exile, once more the slave of a pagan nation that will humiliate it.

How long, Lord, before so many failures and so much death have the power to make us understand what we are without you?

But so much human madness is possible because God’s heart is just as mad: “My thoughts are not your thoughts! Nor are your ways my ways.”

It is true: … and so are his ways!

He swore it to Noah, promised it to Abraham, confirmed it to David: “I will not destroy man.”

With what is no longer a people, a holy nation, with a small “group” of dejected and despairing exiles, God will begin again. Ezekiel will be the “consoler” and the “teacher” of a “remnant” that will accept the proposal: “I shall give you a docile and obedient heart.”

For hope to be born again, in fact, a new heart will be needed, the heart of a child. That “remnant” will welcome that ancient promise: “I shall be your God!”

And in the small womb of the “remnant”, the covenant will be fulfilled: the Messiah will be given. That “King” who is destined to rule all the nations with a strong arm. He will gather up broken and contrite hearts, bind the wounds of an exhausted humanity and present to God, for all of us, a pure and innocent heart. An obedient heart.

Then he will enter the Sanctuary of “heaven” once for all, to gather for ever an inheritance that we have longed for since the beginning of the world.

An eternal covenant, the only one, the one that Jesus has obtained and gives to the world.

Blessed, then, are those invited to his banquet, to his royal table.

Blessed be he who lives and reigns as Lord for ever and ever. Amen.

1ST CELEBRATION

GOD REVEALS HIMSELF TO THE PROPHET ISAIAH

Introduction to the celebration

Isaiah sees God as a king seated on a high and lofty throne, clothed in the royal mantle, revealing himself to him at a particular moment in history and in a precise place: the Temple of Jerusalem.

If God has revealed himself to Isaiah, it means that this is a time of salvation, the right time fixed by him to intervene and save his people. In the person of Isaiah, chosen, consecrated as a prophet and made able to proclaim his holiness, the Lord visits his people, wants to open the eyes of his children, wants to offer his covenant once again in spite of the many unfaithfulnesses of his people.

In the person of M. Rosa too, raised up by God in our time, the Lord has shown his kindness and has recalled to the Church the Mystery of his mercy, manifested in Mary, conceived “Immaculate” in the womb of Anne. This prerogative of divine mercy – the widest and most tangible expression of his faithfulness – he wished to entrust to Mother Rosa, calling her in the Church to become herself mercy together with him, thus continuing and embodying his own mystery.

The invitation to walk in communion with God thus becomes a reality in the call of the Movement to live, in the Church, the Covenant – the Hope of the prophets of Israel and of the Remnant of Yahweh.

Theological commentary on the biblical reading

A vision that reveals the transcendent holiness of God and the radical wretchedness of the creature.

A light on our humanity, unable to reach communion with God and to proclaim his beauty, his greatness, his omnipotence…

God’s initiative will be necessary: “…no one knows the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him” (Mt 11:27).

A vision, a message, a revelation that announce a gift: although fallen, man by grace can stand in God’s presence, see him and… not die, indeed…

But a hard and difficult… path is also announced: a wearisome pilgrimage through deep purifications and exiles of the heart, which will teach us to persevere in waiting for a liberation deeper than that of Israel from Egypt.

1st Reading: Isaiah 6 (in place of the Short Reading of the Breviary)

(brief pause of silence)

Listening to Mother Rosa

Mother Rosa, like Isaiah, is aware of the faithful love of God, who draws to himself with renewed tenderness a fragile humanity constantly in need of forgiveness.

2nd Reading: from Spiritual Physiognomy, pp. 53–54; 60

(passages from the Memoirs)

• Guiding questions for personal reflection and sharing in the group

• Are you aware of the purifications through which M. Rosa passed in her life, and how everything served to strengthen her fidelity and her filial surrender to the action of God, which led her to identify herself with her beloved Crucified One?

• How many “angels” will be needed in our life, so that every least murmur may be taken away from our lips and we may begin to open ourselves to divine praise?

• When will our heart, purified also by sufferings, learn fidelity and filial surrender to the action of God? When at last will hope be so deeply rooted in us that it never disappoints again?

• How many times do you too abuse your freedom, believing yourself able to reach your goal independently of God, and so breaking the covenant that he has made with you?

2ND CELEBRATION

GOD’S FREE INITIATIVE

(God’s unpredictable calls)

Introduction to the celebration

It is not enough to be descendants of Abraham or of Israel in order to be heirs of the covenant: God has the free initiative to choose, within the sinful history of human beings, those who will bring his plan of salvation into the world.

His sovereign freedom goes against every expectation, and works effectively in those who believe and accept his mercy, not as a good to be won, but as a grace to be received through faith.

By intervening personally, and on many occasions, in human affairs, God progressively becomes the author of that work of grace which will be accomplished in Christ Jesus.

• Celebration of Evening Prayer (or Morning Prayer or another Hour of the Office)

• Invocation of the Holy Spirit (in place of the Hymn)

• Psalms and Canticle

Theological commentary on the biblical Reading

We can hope without being disappointed, as Paul teaches us (Rom 5:5), because the Holy Spirit is given to us out of the Father’s love. It is only thanks to God, then, that we can withstand all the trials and difficulties of the “path” and… aim at “holiness”. But take care: it is God who takes the initiative; he chooses, and we cannot delay or put off his invitation.

Our conversion is a mysterious work of his mercy.

1st Reading: Romans 9

(pause of silence)

Listening to M. Rosa

M. Rosa recognises the free and loving initiative of God in her life; she does not harden her heart before God’s interventions, she lets herself be shaped by him, she trusts him.

2nd Reading: from Spiritual Physiognomy, p. 139 (passage from the Memoirs).

Points for reflection

• Does it not seem to you that the prophets and the Apostles invite us not to undervalue the gift of faith, by which we too, pagans by birth, have been brought into the history of salvation, of which Israel was the protagonist?

• Does it not seem to you that the hardening into which the chosen people fell can become a danger for us too, when we neglect the teaching of Sacred Scripture and do not sufficiently value the need to deepen, through prayer, our knowledge of spiritual realities?

• Do you value your baptism as a sign of the covenant that God has made with you?

• Has there also been in your life, as in M. Rosa’s, a moment when God’s mercy drew a dividing line between a past to be wiped out, because it was still directed towards the earth, and a call to a journey of faith that helps you to discover the Lord as the supreme good, for whom it is worth living?

3RD CELEBRATION

SALVATION, GOD’S CONSTANT CONCERN

Introduction to the celebration

God’s covenant with man is possible only because God has granted man the ability to accept his gift.

This covenant (salvation) is neither added to creation nor superimposed on it, nor does it happen outside it or without relation to it, but it is its fulfilment.

• Celebration of Evening Prayer (or Morning Prayer or another Hour of the Office)

• Invocation of the Holy Spirit (in place of the Hymn)

• Psalms and Canticle

Theological commentary introducing the hearing of the Word

There is only one God, who created the whole universe. Because they forgot this, many peoples strayed, and still stray, from the truth, ending in ignorance and idolatry…

Neither “chance”, nor “matter”, nor “demons”… not even “angels” hold the destiny of the world in their hands…

No force, however evil, will be able to destroy the good that God, our Father, has created for us, to fill “our hearts with delight”.

He has sworn with an eternal pact… that death will not have the last word!…

1st Reading: Acts 14:8–18

(brief pause of silence, for interiorisation)

Listening to Mother Rosa

Mother Rosa contemplates, in all its beauty and its qualities, the spectacle of the earth, celebrates the marvels that characterise the creation God has given to the people, and lives all this as a place prepared by God for humanity’s meeting with him.

2nd Reading: from Trials and Consolations, p. 65 (see Appendix, Annex no. 1)

Guiding questions for personal reflection and the sharing in the group that follows.

• In her journey with God, day by day, M. Rosa learns that “in the work of the Lord philosophy, theology and calculation have no place; they are all empty lecture chairs…”: the only important science is learning to do the will of God.

How did she come to learn this science?

• Are you convinced that history and the universe are in God’s hands? Or are you afraid and worried that the forces of evil may have the last word?

How much do you keep of that constant and repeated teaching of Jesus: “Do not be afraid, I have conquered the world”?

• Sharing

• Canticle of the Magnificat (or another)

• Intercessions (from the Breviary or spontaneous)

• Our Father

• Concluding prayer

For further personal reflection (at home)

The Apostles call us to turn away from vanities… Read Romans 1:18–32. Everything becomes vanity if you despise the “knowledge of God”.

Read also what Paul preaches at Athens: Acts 17:22–34. The time of ignorance is now past… There is a command to repent… There is a future judgement that admits no excuses…

• Are you willing to walk with those who want to… “live, move and have their being in God”?

• Do you want to follow your own wisdom and be abandoned to your passions, which will lead you to death?

4TH CELEBRATION

GOD’S JUSTICE AND MERCY

Introduction to the celebration

Every time violence tends to bring the world back into chaos, God intervenes with his commitment, his “promise”, to guarantee the order of the cosmos and to save the world from destruction, choosing people capable of walking in his presence and doing what he commands.

Thus the hope of salvation is rekindled.

God provides for himself within humanity a “remnant” that fulfils its mission on behalf of all and so becomes an instrument of salvation for others.

Noah represents this “remnant” of humanity that ensures human survival.

These marvellous interventions of God will nourish the meditation and the life of Anne and Mary, as they had already nourished that of the little “remnant” of Israel, which loved constantly to remember everything that God had done and promised, nourishing in him alone the hope of salvation.

St Anne lived this hope in trusting expectation of definitive salvation, and with her Mary, “a sign of hope for humanity persecuted by evil” (Revelation 12:1).

• Celebration of Evening Prayer (or Morning Prayer or another Hour of the Office)

• Invocation of the Holy Spirit (in place of the Hymn)

• Psalms and Canticle

Introduction and theological commentary on the biblical reading

Great is the wickedness of men! Even the saints have felt in their hearts the heaviness of this situation. Isaiah himself, a man chosen by God, felt that he would have been lost, had God himself not upheld him…

And this corruption seems (if that were possible) to embitter the very heart of God: “…the Lord regretted having made man on the earth, and his heart was grieved”…

But take note: a single man was enough to console that divine heart: Noah.

God is always looking for a “womb” that can welcome him… into which he can pour his blessings!

1st Reading: Genesis 6:5–22

(pause of silence for interiorisation)

Listening to the experience of M. Rosa

M. Rosa recognises the absolute primacy of God in her own life, in her affections, in her possessions.

She suffers and willingly offers herself to God, neither taking offence, nor losing heart, nor despairing at the evil that surrounds her… but works with greater care and commits herself with more love for the benefit of all.

2nd Reading: from Trials and Consolations, p. 62 (in the Appendix, Annex no. 2)

(pause for silence and personal reflection)

Guiding questions for personal reflection

• What do you understand by “God regretted having made man”?

• Jesus too took a severe attitude towards this perverse and adulterous generation of ours.

• Do you believe that you are a sinner? Not better than your father? Do you understand that your mistakes and your selfishness have a deep and mysterious effect on those around us, in the very society in which we all live?

Read Psalms 14 and 53 and Romans 7:7–25

5TH CELEBRATION

GOD’S COVENANT WITH NOAH

Introduction to the celebration

Man, who at the dawn of his existence had already known the great peace of meeting with God, lives it again after the dramatic experience of the flood, in the setting of a pacified nature, thanks to God’s intervention and to the covenant he offered to Noah.

God neither forgets nor retracts the first promise made to Adam in Paradise; indeed he saves his creation and brings it where he wishes, even though man’s heart remains wicked.

His action seeks the salvation of sinful humanity, purifying it and almost creating it anew.

Before God, Noah is regarded as the representative of all human beings, a figure of Christ, the one truly sent into the world for the salvation of the whole of humanity, an example of unshakeable faith and sure hope in God’s definitive judgement.

• Celebration of Evening Prayer (or Morning Prayer or another Hour of the Office)

• Invocation of the Holy Spirit (in place of the Hymn)

• Psalms and Canticle

Introduction and theological commentary on the biblical reading

God remembered Noah…

God is faithful! Whoever walks with him is not lost… does not remain alone…

When the wind of the Spirit descends on the earth, the waters of death… subside!

We must always wait to be clothed with this power and strength that come from him (cf. Luke 24:49). Even if the waters seem to submerge us.

But take note of what Noah does: with him God makes a covenant!

Thanks to him, for all of us there is that eternal word: “Never again will I curse the earth!”..

Noah builds an altar and offers burnt offerings… He takes every kind of first fruits…

Once more there are altars to be built in our hearts, in our homes, in our cities, in our nations… altars from which a fragrance pleasing to God may rise.

Once more our supplications, our groans, our praises, our expectations must rise to God…

Our offerings must be consumed without weariness… that is, given to God with joy. Without fear. Only in his goodness can we trust and hope and wait for his peace, his blessing… “Lift up your hearts!”… This is the burnt offering.

1st Reading: Genesis 8

(brief pause for interiorisation)

In comparison with M. Rosa

The covenant, a meeting between God and man, is an essentially free gift of divine love

Like Noah, M. Rosa too lives and expresses great devotion towards God, makes her life an unceasing worship of God and offers herself as a victim for the sins and the salvation of the world.

2nd Reading: from Trials and Consolations, p. 207 (in the Appendix, Annex no. 3)

(brief pause of silence)

Personal reflection, helped by the following questions

• Are you convinced that whoever walks with God is not lost?

• Do you trust solely in his goodness, hope for and wait for his peace, his blessing, his mercy?

6TH CELEBRATION

A COVENANT SEALED IN THE PROPHETIC SIGN OF THE RAINBOW

Introduction to the celebration

God speaks, sets his bow in the clouds, establishes the covenant, intervenes on behalf of the world, announces that there will be no more flood.

The covenant with Noah, of which the rainbow is the sign and prophetic message, extends to the whole of creation and represents God’s first great promise of salvation for humanity and the whole world; it becomes the first prophetic announcement addressed to all human beings.

By virtue of this covenant – a wholly free expression of the divine initiative – the created world and humanity walk under the visible sign (the rainbow) of a promise of salvation.

All of God’s teaching is aimed at this covenant.

• Invocation of the Holy Spirit (in place of the Hymn)

• Psalms and Canticle

Theological commentary on the biblical reading

We are all descendants of that ark saved from the flood; we have all been drawn out of a great tragedy and benefit from that promise: No flood will ever again devastate the earth!… When you see the rainbow shining, remember… God is with us!

He will continue to bless us… For ever!

It is a promise that reaches even beyond this time, this earth, this sky…

For we shall see new heavens and a still more splendid earth!

1st Reading: Genesis 9:8–17

Comparison with M. Rosa

An important condition for entering into the covenant with God is obedience, submission, a faith open to hope, the acceptance of the new life that he gives, setting out again on the journey with him.

M. Rosa experienced all this in her life

2nd Reading: from Trials and Consolations, p. 423

(in the Appendix, Annex no. 4)

Personal reflection and sharing.

Letting ourselves be challenged by the word of God and by the deep experience of M. Rosa, let us ask ourselves:

• Am I open to the Lord and to the covenant with him, docile and humble before his will, which wants to make itself present through me too, today, in history, with the gift of peace, communion, harmony and providence?

• Do I too feel myself a descendant of that “ark”, saved from the flood of the passions?

• Do I keep in mind that God is a Father and does not love to destroy his creatures, but has established an eternal covenant with me too?

7TH CELEBRATION

KEEPING THE PROMISE

Introduction to the celebration

God is always faithful to his people, to his pact.

A fundamental element of the covenant is to take account of God’s faithfulness and to rely on it.

The whole of biblical history is the history of God’s loving presence and of his interventions of mercy on behalf of Israel, the people he chose for himself and wishes to lead into covenant with himself through a teaching that gradually matures.

The Poor, the remnant of Israel, among them St Anne and Mary Immaculate, are aware of this: open to the Lord and sure that God accompanies us, guides us and completes the journey with us, they cultivate praise in their hearts and, living in the world, bear witness to the truth that must be fulfilled: “new heavens and a new earth”, the realisation of the Kingdom of God, the fulfilment of his will.

• Celebration of Evening Prayer (or Morning Prayer or another Hour of the Office)

• Invocation of the Holy Spirit (in place of the Hymn)

• Psalms and Canticle

Theological commentary on the 1st Reading

Have you followed Isaiah’s experience? “The whole earth is full of his glory!” – so he had exclaimed (6:3)!

God’s holiness is the love with which he burns away our miseries and gives us life again. He does not allow our impurities and ugliness to destroy us… He remembers his covenant made with Noah.

Do you remember?

Do you too keep that promise?

The “poor of Yahweh”, the “remnant” of Israel, St Anne… kept it, and saw and tasted the divine tenderness.

The prophets have always encouraged us to look for fulfilments of holiness, manifestations of divine life, ever greater, ever deeper, ever closer to our heart…

Take Isaiah 65:17–18. Do you see the fruits of waiting, of hoping in the one who loves life?

And then Isaiah 66:22. Does not the promise made to Noah echo here?

Everything is prepared for a future reality that will know no sunset and no weariness…

The apostles too, disciples of the Messiah, announced that with his coming the new times had been inaugurated, and that those new heavens and that new earth, the dwelling place of God’s glory, were therefore now close at hand…

Read also 2 Peter 3:13–14 and Revelation 21:1. Take care to keep these promises!

Today it is difficult to open ourselves to this hope. There is too much fear in our hearts.

Life is little loved, and there is no struggle to defend it… Mothers kill hope in their own wombs…

Young couples no longer desire God’s blessing on their home… Fear of remaining faithful… Fear of committing themselves!

Fear of taking on responsibility!

Why is that divine promise neglected: “I will not destroy the earth!” Take note: see instead how the little “remnant” opened itself trustingly to its future…

1st Reading: Isaiah 65:17–18; 66:22

(pause of silence)

In the light of the Spirituality

With the remnant of Israel, and particularly beginning with St Anne, God begins a new history: he opens the path of humanity to universal dimensions of hope. Anne comes to be the temple of the singular manifestation of the Father’s motherhood and mercy, she in whom “all the justices and all the holiness of the old law found their fulfilment; in me rested the groans, the sighs, the tears and the prayers of all the Just of the Old Testament, because from me, as from the most fruitful root of Jesse, sprang my daughter, Mary Immaculate, and Jesus Christ her Son and Son of God, source of the new law of love”.

2nd Reading: from the Statute of the Movement, arts 4–6, pp. 5–7

Mother Rosa, even in the midst of the sufferings and difficulties of every day, does not let herself be cast down:

She believes in divine intervention and in his mercy.

She hopes, waits and works so that every child of God may come to know Jesus and enjoy “the new heavens and the new earth” already here on this earth, living in communion with him.

She contemplates in ecstasy St Anne and, in her, Mary, the new earth chosen by the Father to fulfil the “Hope of Israel”.

Pointers for personal reflection and sharing in the group.

• What lesson do you feel you can draw for your personal life and for your belonging to the Movement?

• Have you too happened to enjoy the divine tenderness, or do you believe that this is impossible? Do you desire it?

• Are there still many fears in your heart? Are you open to life? Do you fight to defend it? Are you afraid of committing yourself, of taking on responsibility?

• Concluding prayer (from a manuscript of M. Rosa)

“Most august Matron, cradle of the beneficent Seed and indeed Source of all hope, co-operator in the New Covenant, your womb was sanctified by the Most Holy Trinity because it was to form the dwelling for the beloved Daughter of the Father, the new Eve.

Tell me what your womb felt at the entering of her who was the delight of the Eternal Father, who had been filled with the Holy Spirit, and whom the Son of God looked upon as Mother and, obedient, showed himself willing to come down and make himself small in order to dwell in her?”

And now, with the same deep joy as Mother Rosa, who contemplates St Anne, joined in Mary to the work of Redemption and to the History of Salvation, let us sing.

8TH CELEBRATION

A HEART OF “LITTLE ONES”, TO CONTEMPLATE GOD AND THE BEAUTIES OF CREATION: TO RETURN TO HIM

Introduction to the celebration

The privileged creature, called into existence by God and willed by him as the “you” of a dialogue of “communion” for a “mission”, is man.

The proper vocation of man – as an individual and as a body of men and women – is to be the image and likeness of God, sharing in “his magnificence, crowned with glory and honour, invested with royal power over the works he has created”.

But man is subject to the temptation to put himself in the place of God in creation. In this act he loses the luminous and objective vision of things, and no longer recognises God.

Only in the simple do the feelings of admiration, praise and gratitude remain, which were constantly present in the heart of St Anne and of Mary.

In the very womb of Anne the original innocence shone out again: the first creation is joined to the second.

• Celebration of Evening Prayer (or Morning Prayer or another Hour of the Office)

• Invocation of the Holy Spirit (in place of the Hymn)

On the threshold of his tent, crouching on the ground, Abraham is absorbed in a dark, bitter silence… “Those stars will still send signals of light when I am no more… They will guide other men, but in search of what? I have had no answer. No god has taken this loneliness from me… and now my strength is ebbing away. Before long I shall be a mystery of emptiness, of nothing… Where will my laments and all my desires find refuge? Where are my days gone by? Where can I find them again? From that inner torment, suddenly a command, a voice: “Go!… walk to where I shall show you… and I will make of you a great people!”

Right there, in that silent darkness, in that defeated halting, under that immense and oppressive starry sky, when man’s reflecting finds no more way out and he is seized by the mortal anguish of his limit and the nothingness of his brief and fleeting existence appears in terror… there, right there, God shows himself “living”.

Abraham cannot fail to sense that those few words, decisive, imperative phrases, which echo within him, do not come from himself. He cannot deceive himself with vain consolations, with other attempts. He is tired, exhausted. He has stopped hoping. Perhaps years before he might still have given himself some encouragement, but not now. That voice is in him, certainly. He has too clearly sensed its origin, but he did not form that thought himself. No… It is a new reality that is appearing to his consciousness. A new life flowing back into his inmost being, which urges him on…

People end by not understanding one another. God promised: I will never again destroy the earth with a flood… But the bitterness of dispersion remains, the difficulty of communicating. Here is the drama of barrenness. We are scattered over the earth, we do not possess it!

Loneliness is multiplied now, not life. And this among peoples, in the family, in the heart of each person. We no longer know how to speak, what to say, often we rave… Man is no longer capable of loving. He does not know how…

Most painful, but precisely in such an experience of deep loneliness and barrenness, God looked with tenderness upon man.

God chooses Abraham.

Let us try to imagine: how much time has passed since God walked with Adam in “paradise”? Who knows. Endless stretches of time and abysmal silences… Humanity, separated from the creative “word”, is plunged in loneliness. Man no longer knows how to communicate, because he no longer knows how to have a creative “word” and can no longer give it to his brother… He is no longer capable of loving. He is scattered, he is corrupted; he knows, painfully, that he is dying.

A longing for good, heart-rending, forces him to go on, to struggle.

The “Law” is written in his heart. He will question himself, he will question the stars, the natural phenomena that tower over him and dismay him…

“Is anyone there?… Who has dominion over certain forces?… Is there a ‘god’?… How can I survive?”

The earth is his enemy, the divinity dark and enigmatic. How will he be able to meet it?

Abraham was a shepherd, a nomad, an ordinary man.

Born, like everyone, in guilt, he already bears in his body the mark of barrenness…

Long years spent without hope: no son gladdens him. His tent without cries of joy. How bitter that hard shepherd’s labour, without the company of the one for whom it makes sense to work: “To whom shall I leave the fruit of my labour?”

Dreams are forbidden… Sarah, his wife, does not wholly fill his heart.

Man is now weak, wounded in memory and in will. Incapable of returning to God, of seeking him, of conversing with him.

He is simply so afraid. He will now have to fend for himself…

God, instead, will slowly have to wait for the right moments to appear in man’s life.

“Now man has become like one of us!” (Genesis 3:22)

Those words: “Go! Walk…” seemed to well up suddenly, from a dark and unexplored place, which was in fact within him.

And how had he never noticed it?

But whose is that voice, which is without sound? Which has so much power over him? He cannot resist it, but perhaps he would not even wish to.

Yes, it frightens him… it drags him into an absurd adventure, impossible for his strength, which he no longer controls, and yet he senses that only in that mysterious command there is something. A glimmer of life?…

Introductory theological commentary on the short reading

Ezekiel will form that “remnant” which, learning the lesson of history, will return to God. It will not rely on human securities, nor place its hope in economic programmes or political alliances. It will once again be faithful to the covenant of Sinai. There Israel was born as God’s “people”. Nehemiah and Ezra will see to the return of the little “remnant” to its homeland. It will be a “remnant”… poor, yet aware of an extraordinary mission. It will have to cast into the heart of the world that irrevocable word: God is One, Faithful, Compassionate; and with the coming of the Messiah it will propose an eternal Kingdom.

The poor are those who, in becoming aware of their own neediness and frailty, discover that Yahweh is the God of the little ones, of the wretched, of the disinherited; and after having experienced in their life his infinite mercy, they abandon themselves trustingly to him, in the assurance that, after suffering, he himself will glorify the humble; and therefore they praise Yahweh and marvel at the works of his arm, expressing in community the joy of their heart. Poverty, a trusting openness to the Lord and a title of right to his love, was the fundamental disposition of the Israel of God, to which St Anne belonged; a disposition that reached its culminating point in Mary; for at the moment of the incarnation she was total openness to the God who was coming to her.

The little “remnant” of Israel presents itself as the proof of a solidarity carried to the highest degree on the basis of humility. The poor are aware that only through the community do they receive life, grace and salvation. It follows that, in the community perspective, this virtue is of the greatest importance for building unity; in fact discord is born of the spirit of domination, of contempt for persons, of envy, of mistrust, of pride and of other selfish passions. And so we cannot be brothers and sisters unless we are united.”(from the Basic Documents of the Daughters of St Anne, ch. II, arts 29; 30; 77)
